paragraphs: MAD-Bayes provides a way to derive scalable algorithms for Bayesian nonparametric models, but its resulting optimization problems can involve difficult discrete choices. Existing practice uses heuristics resembling k-means, which seek local minima. This paper studies an exemplar-based formulation for Dirichlet process mixtures and their hierarchical counterpart, where clustering is organized around representative examples.

The authors replace the combinatorial formulation with a convex optimization problem containing structured regularization. Their key theoretical result is conditional: when the clusters satisfy separation conditions, the relaxed problem has the same optimal solution as the original discrete problem. Under those conditions, the relaxation preserves the desired answer while changing how it can be computed.

An algorithm based on the alternating direction method of multipliers solves the convex program. On the reported benchmark datasets, it finds an optimum of the combinatorial problem and substantially improves the exemplar-based objective relative to existing methods. These findings support the relaxation as a useful alternative to local-search heuristics, with the stated equivalence guarantee tied specifically to cluster separation.
icml-2015-a-convex-exemplar-based-approa.tldr: A convex relaxation solves exemplar-based mixture clustering with matching discrete optima under cluster-separation conditions.

paragraphs: Experience replay lets a reinforcement learning agent reuse past interactions to improve its decisions. It also complicates the distinction between model-based learning and model-free learning: stored experiences can act as an environment model, even when no conventional model is explicitly fitted. This paper investigates that connection at the level of the learning updates.

The authors establish an exact equivalence between the sequence of value functions produced by a particular model-based policy-evaluation method and a model-free method using replay. They also introduce a general replay procedure capable of reproducing methods across a range from TD(0) to linear Dyna. Thus, seemingly different approaches can share the same underlying progression of value estimates.

These relationships motivate forgetful LSTD(lambda), a new model-based algorithm using linear function approximation. The paper reports that it extends more naturally to online control than regular LSTD(lambda). Its multi-step structure also offers an advantage over linear Dyna, enabling good performance in non-Markov settings or problems with substantial function approximation. The contribution connects a theoretical equivalence to a concrete algorithmic design.
icml-2015-a-deeper-look-at-planning-as-l.tldr: Exact connections between replay and model-based evaluation motivate a multi-step algorithm better suited to online control.

paragraphs: Stochastic variational inference makes posterior approximation practical for complex Bayesian models. Its speed, however, does not prevent optimization from settling into local optima. As a result, the quality of the approximate posterior can depend strongly on initialization and hyperparameter choices. The paper addresses this sensitivity by changing the rule used to update the approximation.

The proposed method replaces the usual natural-gradient step with a trust-region update. The central design choice is therefore the way each optimization step is controlled within the inference procedure. The authors report generally better results and reduced sensitivity to hyperparameters, making the update rule relevant to both approximation quality and the effort required to select settings.

The paper also presents a new strategy for variational inference when data arrive as a stream. In that setting, the authors find the trust-region method crucial to obtaining good performance. Together, these results make the update mechanism a substantive part of the inference approach: its reported benefits extend from the original optimization problem to the proposed streaming strategy.
icml-2015-a-trust-region-method-for-stoc.tldr: Trust-region updates improve stochastic variational inference and reduce hyperparameter sensitivity, including in a proposed streaming strategy.

paragraphs: The paper considers a network of nodes that jointly minimize a sum of convex costs. Each node owns its own private cost function, and direct communication is restricted to connected neighbors. This captures distributed learning and sensing problems in which a collective solution must be reached through local computation and communication.

The proposed distributed first-order augmented Lagrangian algorithm, DFAL, has an optimality guarantee for any limit point of its iterates. For a requested accuracy epsilon, the authors also bound the number of outer iterations needed to obtain an approximately optimal and feasible solution. That count grows logarithmically with inverse accuracy, while the total proximal-gradient computations and communications per node have a separate bound involving inverse accuracy and properties of the communication graph.

The authors additionally construct an asynchronous version using randomized block coordinate descent. Experiments on large sparse-group LASSO problems demonstrate DFAL's efficiency. The contribution combines a distributed optimization procedure with guarantees that explicitly account for network structure, making clear that both numerical accuracy and connectivity affect the required work.
icml-2015-an-asynchronous-distributed-pr.tldr: DFAL solves distributed composite convex problems with optimality and complexity guarantees, plus an asynchronous variant.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks model sequences, but training them can be difficult. Long short-term memory networks address that difficulty through a particular architectural design. Their practical success leaves a further question: which parts of that design matter, and could a substantially different recurrent architecture work better? This paper investigates those questions through a large empirical search.

The authors evaluate more than ten thousand recurrent network architectures. They identify one that performs better than both LSTM and the gated recurrent unit on some tasks. The qualification matters: the discovered architecture does not win on every task, so the search provides evidence for task-dependent improvements rather than establishing a universally best recurrent design.

The study also finds that setting the LSTM forget-gate bias to 1 closes the observed gap between LSTM and GRU. This result shows that a small architectural setting can materially affect comparisons between network families. Together, the findings connect broad architecture exploration with a simple adjustment to an established model, clarifying why both design and configuration deserve attention.
icml-2015-an-empirical-exploration-of-re.tldr: A search of over ten thousand recurrent architectures finds task-dependent improvements and a simple LSTM forget-gate adjustment.

paragraphs: Splicing removes non-coding regions from transcribed precursor RNA, making splice-junction prediction relevant to understanding how proteins are produced. The paper addresses weaknesses in the accuracy and robustness of existing computational predictors. It proposes a deep belief network approach with a new training method for restricted Boltzmann machines.

The training method targets class-imbalanced prediction and addresses limitations of conventional contrastive divergence. It also supplies regularization for categorical features. These choices connect the learning procedure to the structure of the prediction problem: the model must handle categorical inputs while learning from classes that are not equally represented.

On public human-genome datasets, the authors report significantly improved accuracy and shorter runtime compared with state-of-the-art alternatives. Their approach is also less sensitive to input-sequence length and more robust to false splice signals. It identifies non-canonical splicing patterns that conventional methods find difficult to recognize. The authors suggest that the method could extend to other subtle genomic structures, presenting that broader use as a future possibility rather than an established result.
icml-2015-boosted-categorical-restricted.tldr: A deep belief network with specialized RBM training improves reported splice-junction accuracy, runtime, and robustness.

paragraphs: Dictionary learning seeks a collection of building blocks that explains observed data through sparse combinations. This paper studies the complete case: the dictionary is square and invertible, and the observations equal that dictionary multiplied by a coefficient matrix. The goal is to recover the underlying dictionary from those observations.

Under a suitable probability model for the coefficients, the authors give an efficient algorithm with a recovery guarantee allowing O(n) nonzero entries per coefficient column. Earlier guarantees allowed only O(sqrt(n)). This expands the level of coefficient density covered by the theory, rather than requiring every observation to use an extremely small fraction of the available building blocks.

The algorithm optimizes a nonconvex objective subject to a spherical constraint. Its analysis characterizes the geometry of that objective and shows, with high probability, that there are no spurious local minima. This explains why nonconvex optimization can succeed in the stated setting. Synthetic-data experiments support the theory, while the recovery claim remains tied to the complete dictionary setting and the specified probabilistic assumptions.
icml-2015-complete-dictionary-recovery-u.tldr: A nonconvex algorithm provably recovers complete dictionaries under a probabilistic model allowing denser sparse coefficients.

paragraphs: Multiclass classifiers may be judged by measures that combine several kinds of correct and incorrect predictions. A confusion matrix records those outcomes, but a performance measure can depend on its entries nonlinearly. This paper develops a framework for learning with such objectives, including multiclass G-mean and micro F1 as well as ordinary loss-based measures.

The main idea is to optimize over the set of confusion matrices that classifiers can achieve. This moves the performance measure into the center of the learning problem. The authors develop two concrete algorithms: one uses Frank-Wolfe optimization for concave measures, and the other uses bisection for measures expressed as ratios of linear functions.

The resulting algorithms are provably consistent, connecting their learning behavior to the intended performance objective. In experiments, they outperform a multiclass adaptation of SVMperf; on large multiclass problems, they are also orders of magnitude faster. The work therefore offers both a general way to organize complex objectives and specific algorithms with theoretical and empirical support for the covered measure families.
icml-2015-consistent-multiclass-algorith.tldr: Optimizing over feasible confusion matrices yields consistent multiclass algorithms for complex measures with strong reported performance and speed.

paragraphs: Independent component analysis aims to recover underlying source signals from observations that mix them together. This paper studies the problem when those observations also contain noise. Its goal includes recovering both the non-Gaussian sources and the mixing matrix, so the result concerns the hidden signals as well as the transformation that produced the measurements.

The authors present consistent algorithms whose running time is polynomial. Their reconstruction error decreases at a rate of 1/sqrt(T), where T is the number of observations, and depends only polynomially on the problem's natural parameters. These guarantees connect increasing data to improving reconstruction while also controlling how computational and statistical difficulty scale.

The analysis further extends to deterministic source signals when their empirical distributions are approximately independent. That extension is central to the title: the sources need not be described only through a random-signal formulation. The stated empirical-independence condition provides the bridge to deterministic signals, preserving a concrete structural requirement for separating the sources from their noisy mixtures.
icml-2015-deterministic-independent-comp.tldr: Polynomial-time ICA algorithms recover noisy non-Gaussian sources and extend to deterministic signals with approximately independent empirical distributions.

paragraphs: Concentration inequalities describe how strongly a random quantity stays near its typical value. This paper develops such bounds for functions of dependent variables, where relationships among observations must be accounted for. That setting matters for learning problems in which the quantities entering an analysis cannot reasonably be treated as independent.

The work extends approaches based on the Laplace transform and fractional graph coloring, alongside approaches using the entropy method. Its new inequalities apply to function classes called fractionally sub-additive and fractionally self-bounding. These structural conditions identify the kinds of functions covered by the results. The paper also proves a new Talagrand concentration inequality for fractionally sub-additive functions of dependent variables.

The contribution supplies mathematical tools for controlling fluctuations when dependence is present. The authors identify generalization analysis as a possible application, including bipartite ranking, where dependent variables arise naturally. They frame such generalization bounds as a prospect enabled by the results; the stated achievement is the collection of concentration inequalities and the associated extension of existing analytical methods.
icml-2015-entropy-based-concentration-in.tldr: New concentration inequalities handle structured functions of dependent variables and could support future generalization bounds.

paragraphs: A determinantal point process assigns probabilities to subsets of a collection of items. In the discrete setting, these probabilities are controlled by a positive semidefinite matrix called the kernel. Learning a DPP from observed data therefore requires estimating that matrix. This paper focuses on making the kernel-learning step simpler and faster.

The authors introduce a fixed-point algorithm and compare it with earlier approaches. They report that the method is substantially simpler while reaching local maxima that are as good as, and sometimes better than, those found previously. The reference to local maxima is significant: the claimed improvement concerns the quality of the solutions obtained by the learning procedure.

Experiments on both real and simulated data illustrate the algorithm's numerical behavior. For large problems, the reported runtime improvement is an order of magnitude. Taken together, the findings suggest that a relatively simple update procedure can provide a favorable combination of computational speed and solution quality, making kernel estimation more practical without sacrificing the reported quality of the fitted DPP.
icml-2015-fixed-point-algorithms-for-lea.tldr: A simple fixed-point method learns DPP kernels with comparable or better local maxima and much faster reported large-problem runtimes.

paragraphs: Large matrix problems are often accelerated by representing a matrix through low-rank factors and applying stochastic gradient descent to those factors. This strategy appears in matrix completion, subspace tracking, and semidefinite-program relaxations. The resulting optimization is nonconvex, making convergence to a global solution a central theoretical question.

The paper supplies a step-size scheme for SGD on a low-rank least-squares problem. Under broad sampling conditions, the authors prove global convergence from a random initialization. For constant-rank problems, the stated bound is O(epsilon^-1 n log n) steps with constant probability. The guarantee therefore specifies both a computational rate and the probability level at which successful convergence is established.

The modification also connects SGD to stochastic power iteration, providing a relationship between the optimization method and another matrix-computation procedure. Experiments illustrate runtime and convergence behavior. The result gives theoretical backing to a particular low-rank optimization strategy, with its scope determined by the least-squares formulation, sampling conditions, and constant-rank setting used in the bound.
icml-2015-global-convergence-of-stochast.tldr: A tailored SGD step-size scheme achieves probabilistic global-convergence guarantees for a low-rank least-squares problem.

paragraphs: A policy-improvement method needs to address more than whether a proposed policy looks promising on available data. This paper develops a batch reinforcement learning algorithm that attaches a probabilistic performance guarantee to each policy it proposes. The user specifies a performance floor and a confidence setting rather than relying on expert-tuned hyperparameters.

More precisely, the algorithm bounds the probability that it returns a policy whose performance falls below the selected floor. The abstract defines that failure-probability bound using the user's specified confidence level. This gives the user a direct way to express an acceptable performance requirement together with a bound on the chance of violating it.

The authors also build an incremental procedure that repeatedly applies the policy-improvement algorithm to generate multiple improvements. They demonstrate viability on a small gridworld, mountain car, and a digital-marketing application using real data. These examples support the practicality of the approach, while the central contribution is the explicit probabilistic connection between proposed policies and a user-chosen performance requirement.
icml-2015-high-confidence-policy-improve.tldr: A batch RL algorithm proposes policies with user-specified probabilistic performance guarantees and supports repeated policy improvement.

paragraphs: Periodic population counts reveal how many individuals are present at observation times, but leave arrivals and departures between those times hidden. This paper studies how to infer those hidden events and population size throughout time. Its probabilistic model applies both to an M/G/infinity queue and to transient ecological populations such as short-lived insects.

Earlier ecological work used maximum likelihood with a simplifying independence assumption that prevented inference about unobserved arrivals and departures. The authors instead formulate a latent-variable model that retains the relevant likelihood. Because that likelihood is intractable, they develop a Gibbs sampler based on Markov bases to carry out inference.

The resulting method uses the observed counts to support a more detailed account of the unobserved population process. The authors empirically examine the sampler's convergence behavior and demonstrate finer-grained inference than the previous approach. The contribution is therefore both a modeling change and a computational method: preserving the dependence structure enables questions about hidden events that the earlier simplification could not answer.
icml-2015-inference-in-a-partially-obser.tldr: A latent-variable queueing model and Gibbs sampler infer hidden population events from periodic counts.

paragraphs: This paper studies linear dynamical systems whose parameters have meaningful interpretations within a domain theory, particularly coupled linear oscillators. Learning how those parameters vary can therefore contribute to explanation as well as prediction. The model attributes temporal variation beyond noise to parameter drift and differences across coupled systems to moderating variables.

That modeling choice shifts attention from perturbations of hidden states to changes in the parameters governing the dynamics. It also reduces opportunities for efficient inference, so the authors develop sampling procedures to learn and fit the models. The approach explicitly makes parameter variation part of the phenomenon to be explained.

The evaluation uses physiological measurements from heterosexual couples discussing a potentially emotional topic, with body mass index considered as a moderator. Models predict the final 20% of each test couple's conversation dynamics, with shared parameters learned using held-out data. As a proof of concept, the study supports the hypothesis that BMI affects dynamics for the experimentally selected topic, linking interpretable parameter variation to prediction in that specific setting.
icml-2015-moderated-and-drifting-linear-.tldr: Sampling-based dynamical models explain temporal change through parameter drift and between-system differences through moderators.

paragraphs: In multi-instance multi-label learning, experts label a group of instances without identifying the label of every individual instance. A bird recording, for example, may list the species present while also containing rain or vehicle sounds. When annotation focuses on target classes, these additional instances remain unaccounted for, and even their presence within a group is hidden.

The paper introduces a discriminative probabilistic model that explicitly allows novel-class instances. This changes what the learner must explain: a group's contents can include both labeled target categories and an additional novel category. The method therefore addresses ambiguity about individual labels together with uncertainty about whether novel instances occur at all.

The authors provide an exact and efficient implementation of maximum-likelihood estimation for the model parameters. The fitted model yields an instance-level classifier covering the target classes and the novel class. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets illustrate effectiveness. The key contribution is making unannotated, out-of-target content an explicit part of learning from group labels, rather than leaving it outside the model.
icml-2015-multi-instance-multi-label-lea.tldr: A probabilistic model learns instance-level target and novel classes from ambiguous group-level labels.

paragraphs: Multi-label classification predicts several labels for each input. Under subset zero-one loss, the prediction is assessed as a whole label set, making the structure of label dependence particularly relevant. This paper asks which groups of labels must be handled together to minimize that loss, rather than treating all label relationships as equally important.

The authors identify irreducible factors of the conditional label distribution as the key units. These are subsets that remain together when the distribution is factored given the input features. The factorization divides the original learning task into independent multiclass problems, each covering the joint possibilities within one label group.

The theoretical results characterize and identify these groups for distributions satisfying the Composition property. Within that subclass, the analysis provides a foundation for general multi-label classification procedures and optimal feature-subset selection. Experiments on synthetic and benchmark data support the conclusions. The result connects a precise distributional property to a simpler organization of prediction, while keeping the optimality claims tied to the stated loss and distribution family.
icml-2015-on-the-optimality-of-multi-lab.tldr: For distributions satisfying Composition, irreducible label factors reduce subset-zero-one classification to independent multiclass problems.

paragraphs: Online boosting aims to convert a weak online learner into a strong one as learning proceeds over time. The paper begins by introducing a definition of weak online learnability that supports this goal. That definition supplies the foundation for two algorithms with different strengths: one emphasizes provable resource efficiency, while the other emphasizes adaptation.

The first algorithm adapts boost-by-majority to the online setting. The authors prove a matching lower bound, showing that its requirements are essentially optimal in both the number of weak learners and the sample complexity needed for a specified accuracy. The lower bound matters because it compares the algorithm's resource use with what the problem fundamentally requires under the framework.

The second algorithm is adaptive and parameter-free, but does not achieve the same optimality claim. The paper thus presents two distinct outcomes within a common theory of online boosting. One establishes how efficiently strong learning can be achieved; the other offers an adaptive procedure without parameter specification, while explicitly retaining the distinction between adaptability and optimality.
icml-2015-optimal-and-adaptive-algorithm.tldr: Two online boosting algorithms offer either essentially optimal resource requirements or parameter-free adaptation.

paragraphs: Natural-gradient optimization uses the Fisher information matrix to shape neural-network updates, but handling that matrix efficiently is a major computational challenge. K-FAC addresses this by approximating large blocks associated with entire layers as Kronecker products of two much smaller matrices. This structure makes the approximation efficiently invertible while retaining relationships beyond a diagonal representation.

The resulting curvature approximation is neither diagonal nor low-rank and can even be fully non-sparse. The authors report that computing an update costs only several times as much as an ordinary stochastic gradient, while each update makes substantially more progress on the objective. That tradeoff can make K-FAC much faster in practice than SGD with momentum.

The method also performs well in highly stochastic optimization regimes. A central explanation is that the storage and inversion costs of its curvature approximation do not depend on how much data is used to estimate it. K-FAC therefore combines a richer curvature representation with a cost property often associated with simpler approximations, supporting useful updates even when estimates use limited data.
icml-2015-optimizing-neural-networks-wit.tldr: K-FAC uses Kronecker-factored Fisher approximations to make natural-gradient neural-network training computationally practical.

paragraphs: Dual coordinate descent efficiently solves L2-regularized learning problems such as linear SVMs and logistic regression. Its practical implementation becomes faster by maintaining primal variables while updating dual variables, a strategy used in LIBLINEAR. This paper parallelizes that approach for shared-memory multicore machines, where synchronized alternatives have struggled to obtain good speedups.

PASSCoDe lets each thread repeatedly select a random dual coordinate and update it using shared primal variables. The authors analyze how different locking and atomic-operation choices affect convergence. With atomic operations, they establish linear convergence under mild conditions, providing a theoretical guarantee for a particular way of coordinating shared updates.

For an implementation with neither locking nor atomic operations, the analysis characterizes the converged answer as the exact solution of a primal problem with a perturbed regularizer. This specifies how the result relates to the original optimization objective. Experiments show substantially faster performance than previous parallel coordinate-descent solvers, connecting the reduced coordination requirements to practical speed while distinguishing the guarantees of the different implementations.
icml-2015-passcode-parallel-asynchronous.tldr: PASSCoDe accelerates dual coordinate descent through asynchronous shared-memory updates with guarantees that depend on synchronization choices.

paragraphs: Bayesian learning on sensitive data must balance statistical usefulness with protection for individuals. This paper connects Bayesian sampling to differential privacy, which permits aggregate learning while controlling individual-level privacy exposure. Its first result shows that, under standard assumptions, drawing one sample from a posterior distribution already provides a differential-privacy guarantee.

The same sample can serve as a statistical estimator. The authors state that it is often consistent, near optimal, and computationally tractable, linking privacy to useful estimation rather than treating privacy as an entirely separate processing step. The qualification about assumptions and the focus on one posterior draw are part of the stated result.

A separate result concerns stochastic-gradient methods for Hybrid Monte Carlo sampling. The authors show that these methods can preserve differential privacy with minor or no procedural changes, leading to an anytime Bayesian-learning algorithm under a privacy constraint. On synthetic and real datasets, the resulting approach substantially outperforms the compared state-of-the-art private methods. The work identifies sampling randomness as a source of both statistical computation and privacy protection.
icml-2015-privacy-for-free-posterior-sam.tldr: Under stated assumptions, posterior sampling provides differential privacy, and stochastic-gradient Monte Carlo supports practical private Bayesian learning.

paragraphs: Matrix completion becomes a different learning problem when observed entries contain only positives, such as likes or friendships, and no confirmed negatives. Unobserved entries remain unlabeled. This paper treats that situation as positive-unlabeled learning and develops recovery methods under the assumption that the underlying matrix has bounded nuclear norm.

The authors distinguish two observation models. When the matrix specifies a distribution that generates binary entries, shifted matrix completion recovers the underlying matrix using observed ones. When thresholding produces the binary matrix, biased matrix completion instead recovers that thresholded matrix. Matching the recovery target to the observation mechanism is central to the formulation.

The paper derives error guarantees and states that, for a dense large n-by-n matrix, O(n log n) observed ones suffice for small error. It also extends the analysis to settings with row and column features. Efficient optimization procedures are evaluated on semi-supervised clustering and link prediction, including networks exceeding two million nodes and ninety million links. The findings combine recovery theory with evidence of scalability for positive-only observations.
icml-2015-pu-learning-for-matrix-complet.tldr: Positive-unlabeled matrix completion provides recovery guarantees and scalable algorithms for learning from observed ones without confirmed zeros.

paragraphs: Lifelong reinforcement learning seeks agents that accumulate knowledge across tasks and use it to learn new tasks more quickly. The paper identifies two shortcomings in existing methods: regret that does not vanish with increasing experience, and limitations that can produce suboptimal or unsafe control policies. It develops a policy-gradient learner to address both concerns.

The algorithm learns multiple tasks online in an adversarial setting while enforcing safety constraints on the policies it learns. This places constraints within the learning process itself. The objective is to retain the benefits of accumulating experience across tasks while controlling which policies the learner can produce.

The authors establish sublinear regret for lifelong policy search. Sublinear growth means that cumulative regret increases more slowly than the learning horizon, so regret per step diminishes as experience grows. They also validate the method on benchmark dynamical systems and a quadrotor-control application. The contribution combines a long-run learning guarantee with explicit policy constraints and empirical control demonstrations, with safety expressed through the constraints enforced by the algorithm.
icml-2015-safe-policy-search-for-lifelon.tldr: A lifelong policy-gradient learner enforces safety constraints while achieving sublinear regret in an adversarial online setting.

paragraphs: Natural-gradient methods become difficult to apply in high dimensions because their updates require approximately solving large linear systems. This paper introduces FActorized Natural Gradient, or FANG, to make those updates cheaper. The approach approximates the Fisher information matrix through a Gaussian graphical model whose precision matrix can be computed efficiently.

The authors study the Fisher matrix of a small restricted Boltzmann machine and derive an extremely sparse graphical model. That model closely matches the covariance of the sufficient statistics examined in their analysis. The important design idea is to exploit structure in the approximation so that the matrix operation needed for natural-gradient learning becomes more manageable.

Experiments indicate that FANG trains restricted Boltzmann machines more efficiently than stochastic gradient descent. The analysis also provides insight into why the centering trick works surprisingly well for RBM training. Together, these contributions offer both an approximate optimization method and an explanation of an existing training practice, grounded in the structure of the Fisher matrix investigated in the paper.
icml-2015-scaling-up-natural-gradient-by.tldr: FANG uses a sparse graphical approximation to make natural-gradient RBM training more efficient in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Subspace clustering groups data drawn from several underlying subspaces, but missing entries prevent classical methods from being applied directly. Completing the whole data matrix first is also problematic: data spread across multiple subspaces may have high overall rank. This paper develops two approaches that address clustering and completion while accounting for that structure.

The first extends sparse subspace clustering to construct a sparse representation using only observed entries. The second assumes a random model for missingness, estimates a suitable kernel matrix, and obtains the sparse representation from that kernel. These approaches provide different routes to the information needed for clustering incomplete observations.

Experiments on synthetic and real data reveal advantages and disadvantages of the proposed methods. All outperform low-rank matrix completion followed by sparse subspace clustering when the data matrix is high-rank or a large share of its entries is missing. The finding identifies conditions where handling incomplete data within the clustering approach is empirically preferable to relying on global low-rank completion as a preliminary step.
icml-2015-sparse-subspace-clustering-wit.tldr: Two methods cluster incomplete subspace data and outperform completion-first clustering in reported high-rank or heavily missing settings.
